p: Thank you for your response and, um, my last question, uh, serving, uh, on the, uh, Conflict of Interest Board requires a strong, uh, commitment to impartiality and maintaining public trust, which is so important. Uh, what motivates you personally, uh, to continue serving, uh, in this role and how do you approach, uh, that responsibility?

Well, uh, uh, to be candid, I, I, I, I, I do enjoy the work. Um, uh, and, um, I find it interesting. I find city government interesting. Uh, and, um, and I, I have a lot of respect for the

people who work there and the people who are on the board. Um, and, um, uh, let me, let me put it this way. I- I don't have any trouble being a straight shooter. I call them like I see them. I'm honored to have been, uh, nominated by, uh, Mayor de Blasio. I'm honored to be nominated now by, uh, Comptroller Levine. But, um, uh, everybody that comes before me is gonna be the same whoever appointed me.
Alright, thank you. Thank you, Madam Chair.
Thank you. We also have been joined by Majority Leader Abreu, and now I'd like to turn it over to, um, Minority Leader Carr for his questions.

Thank you, Chair. Mr. Hawley, good to see you. Thank you for coming before us today. Um, I want to just, uh, double down on the question my, my colleague just asked you about impartiality. Um, you know, obviously, uh, everybody comes to their role in government with a lifetime of views and well-developed and passionately believed in. Um, I'm sure you're no exception to that. Um, and so, you know, but there's a diversity of opinion in this city, you know, from left to right. And I

just want you to expound a little bit about, you know, how you feel, uh, you would be able to sort of check your own well-developed views at the door when folks come before you um, who may come from a, a different perspective?

Let me offer my experience, and, and I, um, um, and, and this is, um, this is perhaps even more the case over the last, uh, 5, 6 years now that we've had, uh, the board has had appointees both from the, uh, uh, Comptroller and the Public Advocate as well as only the Mayor. The notion of who, uh, appointed somebody has, has never been reflected in any way, in any kind of favor, any kind of flavor. Um, um, the notion of who appointed somebody, frankly, never really crosses anybody's mind. The, the board and the people on - that work at the board and the people who serve, uh, the board, serve as members of the board, I think owe their loyalty to that institution and to the city, to all the people of the city, and to treat everybody alike. Now, do some people vote for somebody and some people vote for somebody else? I have no idea who people voted for, or really even— I, I don't wanna be naive, could I guess some, some people's political

party, but I don't know that for a fact about many of the people who've been on that board over the years. Um, um, we certainly respect the diversity of the city and people will have different views, but really, um, um, it's a, it's an apolitical body is I think the best way I can put it. It's, it’s meant to be, you know, in something that some people suggest not all, uh, courts can always do. Not all, um, adjudicated bodies can do, but I, I think the board has done a pretty good job about that. Um, uh, I was appointed by, um, Mayor de Blasio. Um, I was on the board during the period of time when we ended up with a disposition that, uh, is causing now the former Mayor to make quarterly payments of about $15,000 on a very significant amount that he owes the city. Um, um, I didn't have any trouble, um, uh, exercising my responsibility in that regard.

Appreciate your answer. Apolitical, that's the- the magic word, uh, I think we were all looking for. So, well- well said. Um, so the, uh, with respect to, um, some other questions, uh, you know, I, I had asked your now new colleague, uh, Mr. Lofredo, uh, this question as well.

You know, COIB operated what I thought was one of the most engaging social media presences, um, er, on, on what was then known as Twitter and, and now X. Um, and then, you know, for whatever reason that social media account ceased to be active or disappeared. Um, obviously education about the conflicts of interest law is one of COIB's core responsibilities, and it's one that it's done very well over the years. Um, it's something I think we should see return, um, because X is a well-trafficked platform. Um, is that something you'd agree with, something you'd look into, and could you shed any light onto why that changed given your long history at COIB?

Yeah, I, I, I, I happened to see that, that exchange with Mr. Lofredo. Um, and, and I, I won't, I, I, I, I'll, I'll plead as, as, uh, he did, but I will not, I, I will also answer the question. Um, but I'll, I'll preface it, uh, as he did by, um, um, uh, expressing a lack of complete familiarity with Twitter and its current incarnation. Um, um, I, I think that may have happened when I was not on the board. Um, in any case, um, there was a little bit of a flight from Twitter at that time.

Um, and, uh, and we valued— I'm talking about in the, in the aughts, uh, certainly in, into the, uh, in, into the second decade of the century, not everything about that, uh, training education unit, stellar. And I think reaches people in a lot of ways. Um, uh, and, and that's important. So whether that's a, that's a decision that needs to be, uh, reversed, I'd at the very least, um, commit to, uh, urging my fellow board members to, uh, go back to staff and say, think about this one. Think about this one. And is it maybe time to go back to, uh, to the, uh, the former Twitter, now, now back to X?
Yeah, I think the- the point you made about the training unit kind of going where they need to go— you meet people where they are.
Yep.

And social media is no different. So I think that that's, uh, a decision worth revisiting, and I appreciate your commitment to having that discussion. Um, and my last question is with respect to establishing a schedule of fines and penalties. I

know this is a much talked about topic, and there's some, you know, discussion about whether or not, you know, over the course of time, uh, over a great different matters that share some, uh, characteristics but are different in other ways, right? No case is ever the same per se, but there are strong similarities that I think should breed some level of consistency. Um, do you think that we should st— that there should be such an establishment of schedules and fines to ensure that consi— consistency? And if not, why not? Um, and would you commit to some sort of an inventory of the board's decisions over the years to ensure that there is some level of consistency over like cases? Uh, uh, um, I, I'm reluctant to commit to, uh, er, er, er, anything terribly exhaustive, but I, but I will say this. Um, first of all, let me be candid. I don't think a schedule is a particularly good idea. Um, uh, I, I think the federal sentencing guidelines have proven not to be successful, and, and they're probably— the need for consistency there is perhaps much more understandable where you've got, I don't know the number of, uh, federal district judges that

are in the country, or, or even federal districts are in the country, but dozens and dozens of different geographic locations all that. You're talking about one body here that doesn't hear that many cases a year. And in every case, in every case where a fine is being set, there's discussion about what the appropriate fine ought to be. Uh, and those— these are mostly settlements, and staff will come back with a settlement number, but that's only after the case has been first before the board, and the board will say, okay, we've seen the- the cases you've cited, we get a sense of that. What are the comparable cases? What's the number? And if the number doesn't seem right within those cases, we're gonna say that's a little bit too high or a little bit too low, considering an awful lot of circumstances. And I think that's really the problem, is, is, is, I think, assuring people that we've thought about— we've thought about a variety of factors, not just cases that look kind of on— um, on the threshold, on first appearances somewhat similar but you've got aggravating circumstances, you’ve got mitigating circumstances, and the board— and I have committed to this that I will strongly recommend to the fellow

board members and through them to staff that they put out a list of those mitigating and aggregating factors um, which, which will cause two cases. And you're correct that otherwise, you know, somebody, somebody, uh, uh, er, ah, hmm, no, I don't wanna give an example, but, um, conduct that looks similar, but the fines were different. But as, as, as in fact reflected in, in 80 or 90% of those settlements that we publish, there'll be a list of what caused the board to make it higher or lower, and, uh, a list of those can and should be, uh, made public.

Yeah, I, I, I think that's a wise step because I, I think sometimes, uh, and, and I read those settlements when, when they come out, you know, like, you, it, it pings a memory of something you read in the past and you're sort of at a loss as to why this could have been treated differently. And I think having, having a sense of what happens in the black box of the decision-making process and then gets put out there I think would, would give folks a better understanding of why there might be these differences.
It is, it is a black box, but we try, and, and, uh, we could possibly try better to, to open it up to the degree we're permitted by law to do. Thank you. Thank you, Chair.

Um, thank you. Um, so in December, uh, in December, DOI published a report titled Report on the New York City Conflict of Interest Board's Advisory Opinion and Moonlighting Waivers Practices. Um, you're— you recognize this report?
I, I think so, yes. It's the one that, um, yes.

Okay, so according to DOI, COIB has created an exception to Chapter 68's moonlight provisions, allowing city attorneys to represent organizations that do business with the city as long as no actual conflict of interest exists in the representation. What is the rationale for this attorney exception to the anti-moonlight provisions of Chapter 68?

Uh, um, that's a, that's a, that assumes a collusion I think is not quite either what that opinion said, and if it, that report said, if it did, it's not quite fair. Um, the - the matter in

question, and I, and I don't feel comfortable going too much into the specifics about that matter. There might have been a little bit of disagreement between, um, uh, the Department of Investigation, who are our friends and, and colleagues in city government, and us about, about, ah, an application of a particularly narrow piece of the law. But there's no, ah, attorney exception, um, to get really wonky about it. Um, um, the definition of position is a little, uh, opaque. Um, in part because it begins with a position is a position, and then it goes on from there. Um, um, you might say it's not the, the, uh, the most felicitous of draftsmanship. Uh, but, um, uh, from there, um, Uh-hmm and this is— um, let me just say this. The, the- we respect and appreciate DOI. We respect what DOE's thoughts were when it issued that particular part of the report, and it caused us to reflect on whether uh, they have a point. Um, that said— the issue of to suggest there's been a change would, would suggest that a lot of these matters come before the board. They don't.

So the next time one does, and that may not be for 1 year or 2 or 3 years, um, eh, but— we'll certainly have to think carefully about this when and if that comes up again.

Okay, um, appreciate that answer. What is, um, your position on DI's recommendation that COIB formalizes via rulemaking its position that outside attorneys are not subject to Chapter 68 moonlighting restrictions?

I, I, well, people with all city employees, uh, are, are governed by the Conflicts of Interest Law, and you're no less, uh, subject to it because you have an outside practice of law. So, um, uh, there's no need, there's no need to— if the suggestion is we, we, we should publish your opinion to— that they're not subject, we wouldn't, we would never publish such an opinion because they are subject to the Conflict of Interest Law. So it's a— the question is, in what way are they a subject? And then we've, we've, um, uh, yeah, I think, I think, I think that's enough said.

Okay, uh, different, uh, different line of questioning. According to DOI, COIB has taken the position that advisory opinions

are entirely protected from disclosure, even though Chapter 68 explicitly provides that the board is required to publish its advisory opinions with personally identifying information redacted. What's the legal basis for COIB's position?

Well, um, what the Charter calls for is for uhm, board decisions to be published but with identifying- all identifying characteristics redacted, um, and, and, and the board, um, uh, respects that. What that means though is that there may be an underlying, uh, letter which is private, um, to, to a public servant in question, but, uh, the, um, but that a public opinion should be issued to alert the public to what that, uh, what that decision was, to do it in a way that, that does not identify, uh, the public servant involved. And because of that, the board has already issued two advisory opinions this year, uh, in response to that recommendation from DOI. So we're, we're taking it seriously and we'll continue to do so. Okay. So some will argue that bad actors can exploit the confidentiality advisory guidance by mischaracterizing the guidance they receive when questioned by the press. Would you agree with that?

Um, yeah, bad actors can do a lot of things. Um, um, it's, it's, um, it's, um, it's, it's possible, it's, it's regrettable, uh, but, uh, um, you, I for one always wonder if something that occurs, um, why the person in question isn't called out if, if that's, uh, if that's suspected by, um, uh, by, uh, by the press, by the public. Let us see the letter. Why not? Let's see the letter. But that's a, that's an editorial on my part.

Okay. The State Commission on Ethics in Lobbying and Government has the power to release unredacted information about guidance requested and the advice given when the recipient of such advice engages in misleading, inaccurate, or incomplete public disclosure of such information. Do you think the COIB should have this power?

Um, it's, it's a, it's a, it's a good question because it's, um, it suggests that in my mind it's almost a waiver, uh, situation, that a waiver of the right of confidentiality. Is there a— have you waived your right of confidentiality if you go talking about the opinion, um, whether it's, whether it's mischaracterized or not? Um, um, good

question. Um, uh, I, I suppose if it's only if it's mischaracterized, this, this gets tough because what's, what's a mischaracterization and which is just a slightly more favorable reading than not? Um, you, you, you'd, you'd be surprised if somebody who had the, uh, a, a letter that was generally favorable went out of their way though to, to emphasize maybe anything negative in it as opposed to, uh, the, the generally positive outcome. So anybody who gets a letter that's generally favorable is going to talk about the favorable stuff. I don't know, these are tough and I really haven't thought about it.

Last, last question, uh, on this topic. Mayor Adams reversed a de Blasio-era policy that encouraged City Hall officials to publicly disclose their COIB guidance, claiming that public servants are not allowed to release the guidance they receive because it's protected under the lawyer-client privilege. Based on your understanding of the City Charter, can public servants voluntarily disclose the guidance they receive from the COIB?

Uh, it's, uh, I know of no obstacle in doing that. The, uh, I've always been of the view that if you get a— if you get what is otherwise a private communication from us, that would include private advice to members of the Council or any other public servant of the city, that the recipient is free to disclose those as he or she wishes.

Thank you, and thank you for, um, the answers to the questions. Um, we also have been joined by Council Member Lee, and, um, any other members, any questions? Okay, thank you. I appreciate you coming here today.
Thank you so much.

Seeing no other members who have questions, Mr. Hawley, you're excused. And Miss Valdivia, I invite you to join us at the witness table. Yes, sorry. Yes. The New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission, known as the TLC, was created pursuant to Local Law 12 of 1971 with the goal of developing and improving taxi and limousine service in New York City. The TLC is responsible for the overall transportation policy with respect to for-hire vehicles. The commission establishes certain rates, standards, and criteria

for the licensing of vehicles, drivers, chauffeurs, owners, and operators. The commission includes 9 members appointed by the Mayor with the advice and consent of the Council. The TLC must include at least one member from each borough. TLC members are appointed for a term of 7 years and can serve until the appointment and qualification of a successor. The Mayor designates one TLC member to act as the Chair and the Chief Executive Officer. The Chair has the power to employ, assign, and oversee the officers and employees of the organization. Pursuant to the Charter, the Chair's position is full-time, and the Mayor sets compensation. The Chair currently receives $243,171 annually. No other TLC member receives compensation. By the letter dated February 13th, and pursuant to Sections 31 and 2301 of the Charter, Mayor Mamdani submitted the name of Midori Valdivia for the Council's Advice and Consent to appoint her as a member of the New York City Taxi and Limousine Commission and to serve as the Chair and CEO of the Commission. Since 2022, Ms. Valdivia has been a member of the Board of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, and from 2018 to 2020, she served as the Chief of

Staff to the Chair and CEO of the MTA. In those roles, she has orchestrated MTA's roles in passing congestion pricing, championed the free bus pilot project, oversaw the MTA's $20 billion annual budget. At the same time, she has also operated her own consulting firm, which provides transportation advisory and not-for-profit management services. From 2015 to 2018, Ms. Valdivia has served as a Deputy Commissioner for Finance and Administration, as Assistant Commissioner for Finance Operations of the Taxi and Limousine Commission. From 2008 to 2015, she worked in various roles at the Port Authority in New York and New Jersey. She has been on the board of the Regional Planning Association. She received her bachelor's degrees from Penn State University and master's in public affairs in urban and regional planning from Princeton University. If appointed by the Mayor, she will serve the remainder of the 7-year term that will expire on January 31, 2031. I now recognize the Committee Counsel to administer the affirmation.

Please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and

nothing but the truth in all your statements before this Committee and in answer to all Council Member questions?
I do.
Thank you.
Good afternoon. Miss Valdelvia, I now recognize you to make an opening statement.

Thank you. Good afternoon, uh, Madam Ung and members of the Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics Committee. Thank you for this opportunity. My name is Midori Valdivia, and I'm honored that Mayor Mamdani has nominated me to serve as Chair and Commissioner of the Taxi and Limousine Commission, the TLC. Let me start by acknowledging why I'm here. Transportation is opportunity. For nearly 180,000 drivers, it's how they learn— earn a living and support their families. For millions of New Yorkers, it's access to jobs, healthcare, and education. For passengers with disabilities, it can be true independence. But here's what I've learned: opportunity doesn't just happen. We have to define what kind of system

creates it and for whom and build the infrastructure to make that real. As an immigrant, as a Latina, I've lived this truth with my family across 3 countries. My family immigrated from Peru to Japan, where I grew up in Osaka. I watched little kids run errands because the streets were designed to be safe. Public transit was designed with a vision that everyone participates in society. Then we immigrated to Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and I saw what happens when you don't have that vision every day, when transportation can reflect inequality instead of opportunity. And that taught me the systems we build are choices we make. Not the inevitabilities we accept. I spent over 15 years at that intersection of transportation and opportunity. At the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. More than a decade ago, I saw TLC drivers waiting all day for just one or two fares. There, I had the opportunity to partner with labor leaders who led the fight for the first wage standards for airport service workers. As Chief of Staff for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, a 70,000-strong agency, I aligned the right people on

major infrastructure initiatives such as improving subway countdown clocks and the launch of OMNY, MTA's contactless payment system. And I worked with a large team to shepherd congestion pricing on behalf of the MTA through state legislation, understanding that dependable transit requires sustainable transit. Like TLC drivers, I don't like traffic. No one does. And it was a meaningful way to better our streets. At TLC, I was Deputy Commissioner of Finance and Administration. I helped build the first-of-its-kind accessible wheelchair program using driver incentives that worked. I contributed to the first driver pay study for for-hire vehicles. And I led TLC's first engagement with national regulators on predatory lending practices targeting small medallion owners. Back then, I was reacting to tech companies, to debt, to complaints, instead of asking, what kind of system do we want? One where drivers can work with dignity, economic sustainability, or one where they're trapped? So I'm answering that question now. Today, TLC regulates nearly— a little under 1 million trips a day. That's comparable to an entire transit system of a major American city. The agency is key to how New Yorkers

get to work, healthcare, and opportunity. That's our current role, and it builds on our founding mission of 1971: protect passengers and drivers by setting safety standards and taxi rates. Today, the threat looks a little different: algorithmic platforms that control workers without transparency, extracting value without accountability, and stifling competition. The mission hasn't changed: protect people from exploitation. But who needs protection and from what? That's evolving, and so must we. In the next few years, TLC will answer questions that shape transportation for a generation. How do we protect hundreds of thousands of workers when the market is disrupted or changed? How do we ensure that platforms that use our public streets serve the public good? Those answers won't just determine New York's future. They'll set standards for cities across this country. And that's the opportunity and the responsibility in front of us. I want a transportation system where professional drivers have professional working conditions and economic security, not just to survive, but an ability to build wealth and thrive, and trips that

are affordable and truly accessible for the passengers who rely on them. That every New Yorker can access our services regardless of ability or zip code, and that technology that serves the public good with transparent rules, fair competition, accountability to passengers, drivers, and ultimately our great city. That's Mayor Mamdani's vision, and it's my vision. We came to this through our own experiences— he through organizing with drivers, me through over 15 years of building transportation teams, policies and systems, and now we get to build it together. Here are my 3 priorities and the ways I'll address them. First, pa— uh, driver dignity and passenger dignity. Economic infrastructure and support resources for drivers. Here's what I mean: expanding the Medallion Debt Relief program, catching violations before workers have to file complaints, a comprehensive penalty review, since— the first since 2016, because workers, many of them immigrants like my family, deserve economic security and not outdated practices.

Second, clear standards for corporate accountability and enforcement. TLC should enforce the rules on the books to protect both passengers and drivers, and TLC should set standards before deploying new technology with verified safety data, driver support, and accessibility on day one. Third, a transportation system that works together. TLC regulates a quarter of all public transportation trips in the city, so we must work together as part of this larger transportation system. That means bringing in a taxi driver's perspective on bus lanes, penalties, training them on the rules, for example. Riders don't just experience taxis or buses as separate systems. They just need to get somewhere. And our riders deserve that. One city, one transportation system. I bring both professional expertise and an understanding to this role. My expertise spans bus, subway, aviation, shared mobility. I've served on various boards. And as an immigrant, as a Latina, as a mom, as a transit wife, I understand what's at stake when transportation determines opportunity. Not just as policy, but as lived experience.

My husband worked every single day during COVID as an essential MTA worker, all while I was pregnant. I've watched him over the years navigate workers' compensation issues, struggle to get bathroom breaks because the system was delayed, even with crew rooms and lockers. Taxi drivers and for-hire vehicle drivers, they have nowhere to go. That's what drives me. I work to build a yellow taxi wheelchair-accessible fleet alongside a formidable disability advocacy coalition to reach 50% accessibility, and the TLC has done it. So I know what that change means for my neighbors who rely on these taxis to move freely. I know many of you have fought and continue to fight for the vision of accessibility and driver dignity that I shared. For debt relief, for transparent wages, for resources, for better conditions. Thank you. I want to be a partner in this work. I'm grateful to the TLC team who have maintained this agency's commitment to serving New Yorkers. Our mission has always been clear: set standards for this industry, and the team has done that. So we're not changing TLC's core mission, but we are doubling down on who we protect and what we protect them from. And

together we'll build on the foundation the TLC has maintained, evolving it for the transportation landscape we face today. The choice isn't between innovation and regulation. It's between letting others define our future or defining it ourselves as a government. Transportation determines who has opportunity. TLC can ensure everyone does. And that's my vision. I'm asking for your partnership to make it real. Thank you so much. The City Council has always been a major partner to TLC in appointing commissioners and collaborating on legislation. I'm ready for your questions, um, to answer, uh, about my vision for TLC and the work we can accomplish together.

Thank you for your testimony. We are also now joined by Council Member Krishnan. Um, you just testified that 50% of all yellow caps are now wheelchair accessible. So based on experience, what challenges does TLC face in the effort to make more taxis more accessible for all?

Thank you so much. So, as you may know, there was a settlement, uh, reached with the City of New York around 50% yellow, uh, taxi wheelchair accessibility. Um, I believe it's really

about service. So, the fleet is out there. It is working. But we have to make sure that we're putting the right incentives to make sure that our taxi drivers are fully compensated for the time, effort, but also we need to do further training to ensure and really build bridges among these communities because every d— person deserves transportation and every person deserves to be seen. I think there's a little bit of work to go, um, a little bit of work uh, to do there. I'm excited to dive in. I know one of the concerns that the disability advocates do have is around accessible dispatch. There was an end of an accessible dispatch program that TLC, um, you know, helped to— helped to finalize. Um, so that's something I'm gonna be looking into because service really matters. It's not just about whether the cars are on the road.
Thank you. Do you— Disability advocates argue that the entire Yellow Cab fleet should be wheelchair accessible so that drivers can't ignore anyone hailing a cab. Do you support this mandate?

I think that's something I'm excited to dive into. As you may know, when I was Deputy Commissioner of the TLC, I actually led the accessible program. And so I understand where disability advocates and people with disabilities are coming from. At the same time, time, um, I, I learned, uh, about the high prices of wheelchair-accessible vehicles. So I know how that can be a burden to our small businesses, to drivers. And so maybe this is something where we really have to start thinking about what does the public, what does government need to do, um, to think about closing this gap? Um, so that's something I'm excited to dive into and learn more about.
Do you support mandating that all yellow cabs be electric?

Ah, well, I think in theory, yes, right? I mean, we love electric vehicles, we should have electric vehicles on the road. I also want to be cognizant of where we are in our charging infrastructure journey in the City of New York. Um, the last thing I would want is a customer going into a taxi and because there might have not been charging

vehicle— charging infrastructure available, maybe the person doesn't get to the end of their trip. That really matters. So I really care about kind of transportation operations. So I'm excited to dive into that. Um, I believe that there's also been thinking about universal design as it relates to electric vehicles in the long term. So of course these products are changing. At the same time, I wanna ensure part of the cost model of being a taxi driver and a for-hire vehicle driver. These costs are high. I don't think anyone's surprised that gas prices are going up. I believe, um, this week or last week, there were, um, prominent articles about the cost of vehicles. So I want to take that into account to understand what kind of model would actually work and serve passengers. Disability advocates urge that you not mandate electric vehicles unless you simultaneously mandate wheelchair accessibility. What is your position on these goals? I think, again, it's been a while since I've been at the TLC, so I'm really excited to dive into these issues. Um, I believe they do have a point, right? Um, when I talked about standards for deploying new technology in my

testimony, I talked about how accessibility should be center, um, but again, an EV vehicle that's a wheelchair accessible vehicle in today's market is very expensive. So that's gonna be top of mind for me. What is that cost model that would actually make, um, the economics work if you're a driver? Why is the burden on the driver or a small business? How do we think about, who has the resources in the ecosystem so this can actually be affordable. When Mayor Mamdani talks about affordability, I also think he talks about the affordability for people who are working— working people every single day who are just trying to make a living. So I also— that's just top of mind for me as well. But as a person who's worked on accessibility issues and have learned so much from the disability community. Um, there is something about— to do the work we do in policy, and I'm sure you all think this way too, values really matter, right? What do we value? And so I do value the disability community. I mean it when I say I want everybody to be able to access our trips regardless of ability or zip code.

According to the disability advocates, vendors claim that past efforts to approve accessible vehicles seem designed to prevent competition. Are you aware of these complaints and do they have any merit? And so how would you modify the approval process?

Uh, this is a really great question and it's something I've actually been really interested in improving vendor pools for transportation agencies in particular, the MTA. That is something I worked on because it made, um, the cost of the thing cheaper, right? When you have more competition. So I'm excited to dive in. I don't know the particularities around this complaint, but I do think competition is a part of how we get there.

The MT Access-A-Ride program only allows 1% of its users to have access on demand, requiring most users to call a day in advance and to know exactly when they will need to be picked up from and where they're going. What will you do at TLC to provide on-demand access to wheelchair accessible for hire vehicles to all New Yorkers who qualify for Access-A-Ride?

Um, I love this question because when I was both at the TLC and at the MTA, I'm proud to have been a leader in, um, developing and supporting and championing what we're calling this on-demand program where you can get within, ah, on-demand Access-A-Ride trips in the form of for-hire vehicles and taxis. So I'm really proud of the work I did there. And, uh, I would be interested in expansion of the program.
That's great. Um, I do have more questions, but I'm gonna pass it on to my fellow Council Members. Um, Council Member Banks.

Thank you, Madam Chair. And, uh, congratulations on your nomination. Um, you know, when it comes to— when we talk about affordability, we can't leave out a taxi pay and benefits.
